parsed_answer.content: Designing a Low-Level Design (LLD) for a parking lot is a canonical object-oriented analysis and design (OOAD) problem frequently encountered in senior engineering interviews. To build a robust system, we must dissect the problem into its core domain entities: Classes, Interfaces, and Design Patterns. Classes represent the structural blueprint of our domain model—such as Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, and Payment—encapsulating state and state-transition logic. Interfaces define contractual behaviors and polymorphism, decoupling high-level orchestration from low-level implementations, as seen in pricing strategies or parking spot allocation algorithms. Finally, Design Patterns provide battle-tested architectural solutions to recurring structural and behavioral challenges. For instance, the Singleton pattern manages the exclusive ParkingLot instance, the Factory pattern instantiates varied vehicle types, the Strategy pattern handles flexible pricing and parking assignment, and the Observer pattern broadcasts real-time capacity updates to display boards.

items: Vehicle inheritance hierarchy: Abstract Vehicle class with a size attribute extended by Car, Van, Truck, and Motorcycle, ensuring polymorphic type handling.
Spot-to-Vehicle compatibility mapping: Compact spots accommodate Motorcycles and Cars; Large spots accommodate Vans and Trucks. This requires strategic encapsulation within the ParkingSpot class.
Strategy Pattern for slot allocation: Nearest-to-entrance strategy vs. compact-first strategy implemented via a common ParkingAssignmentStrategy interface.
Concurrency safety via synchronized blocks or ConcurrentHashMap when mutating spot occupancy states across multiple gate entry terminals.

parsed_answer.content: A common production-level pitfall in parking lot design is race conditions during concurrent spot allocation. If two cars enter different gates simultaneously, they might read the exact same free spot from memory before either thread marks it as occupied. Always ensure that spot assignment and state transition happen inside a synchronized block or transactional database boundary using optimistic or pessimistic locking.
